## CLI

> 15 rules

### Flag Vocabulary

`cli:flag-vocabulary` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Define these flags once, with these names, on every command where they are meaningful; language and framework rules may document how to declare them, but must not rename them or add a second spelling (not `--yes`/`-y`, `--force`, `--plan`, `--no-input`, or `--non-interactive`). `-h`/`--help` prints usage to stdout and exits 0. `-V`/`--version` prints `<program> <semver>` to stdout, exits 0, and returns before reading configuration, touching the network, or entering the alternate screen. `-v`/`--verbose` adds diagnostics on stderr. `-q`/`--quiet` suppresses non-essential output but never errors. `--json` writes machine-readable output to stdout with no ANSI or locale-dependent formatting. `--no-color` disables ANSI and must also honor `NO_COLOR`. `-n`/`--no-interaction` never prompts: confirmation prompts are treated as answered and the command proceeds, even when the interactive default would be no. `--dry-run` prints the planned actions, applies nothing, and exits 0. Accept global flags before and after subcommands, show only the canonical names in help, and when `--dry-run` and `--no-interaction` are combined, `--dry-run` wins and nothing is written.

> URLs: [Command Line Interface Guidelines: Arguments and flags](https://clig.dev/#arguments-and-flags), [NO_COLOR](https://no-color.org/)

### Streams

`cli:streams` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Treat stdout as the program's result and stderr as diagnostics: results, data, and machine output go to stdout; progress, warnings, prompts, and errors go to stderr. Detect TTYs independently and never emit color, spinners, or interactive prompts into a pipe. Support `--quiet` to suppress non-essential output and `--verbose` to add diagnostics on stderr unless documented otherwise.

> URLs: [Command Line Interface Guidelines: Output](https://clig.dev/#output)

### Command Grammar

`cli:command-grammar` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Use one consistent grammar, either `tool <verb> <noun>` or `tool <noun> <verb>`, and never mix both. Keep command names short, stable, and pronounceable; use kebab-case for multi-word flags and reserve single-letter flags for frequent options. Accept positional arguments only for the primary subject, put everything else behind named flags, and never give one flag context-dependent meanings.

> URLs: [Command Line Interface Guidelines](https://clig.dev/)

### Errors

`cli:errors` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Errors state what failed, why, and the exact next step in plain language, quoting the offending value and suggesting a valid alternative or `--help`. Print them to stderr, attach a stable error code or support id to unexpected failures, and show stack traces only behind `--debug` or `--trace`. Never blame the user or leave them without a recovery path.

### Exit Codes

`cli:exit-codes` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Exit 0 only on success and non-zero on every failure. Use 2 for usage errors, 1 for general runtime failures, 126 and 127 for not executable and not found, and 128+n for termination by signal n; document any additional codes. Never encode result data in exit codes, and return the most specific actionable code instead of always 1.

> URLs: [POSIX Utility Conventions](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/V1_chap12.html)

### Version

`cli:version` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Every CLI and TUI tool must expose a non-interactive `--version` (and `-V` where the parser supports it) that prints `<program> <semver>` to stdout, exits 0, and returns before reading configuration, touching the network, or entering the alternate screen. Keep one source of truth for the version (package metadata or a build-time constant), include commit or build metadata only when it does not break parsing, and make the reported version match the release artifact and Git tag.

### Accessibility

`cli:accessibility` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Never rely on color alone to convey meaning; pair it with text, symbols, or position. Honor `NO_COLOR`, `TERM=dumb`, and non-TTY output, preserve readable contrast, avoid rapid flashing, and make every interactive flow usable with the keyboard alone. Keep plain-text output useful when read by a screen reader or copied into an issue.

> URLs: [NO_COLOR](https://no-color.org/)

### Help

`cli:help` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Every command and subcommand supports `-h`/`--help` and prints usage to stdout with exit 0: one-line purpose, usage line, positional arguments, grouped options with defaults, a working example, and a link to further documentation. Running a parent command with no arguments prints its help, and the root command offers `--version`. Generate help from the same definitions the parser uses so it never drifts.

> URLs: [Command Line Interface Guidelines: Help](https://clig.dev/#help)

### Interactivity

`cli:interactivity` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Prompt only when stdin is a TTY and never block in CI, cron, or pipes; expose a flag or environment variable for every prompt so the command can run unattended. Confirm destructive or irreversible actions by default, allow `-n`/`--no-interaction` to skip the prompt and proceed, and make prompts cancelable with Ctrl-C (exit 130) without partial writes. Hide secret input and keep secrets out of process arguments and shell history.

> URLs: [Command Line Interface Guidelines: Interactivity](https://clig.dev/#interactivity)

### Output

`cli:output` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Default output is human-readable and scannable: aligned columns, records that never wrap into each other, and a final summary for batch work. Offer `--json` or `--format` with a stable, documented schema, one record per line, no decoration, and no human-only text on stdout. Honor `--no-color` and `NO_COLOR`, and degrade to ASCII when the locale or terminal cannot render Unicode.

> URLs: [NO_COLOR](https://no-color.org/)

### Configuration

`cli:configuration` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Resolve configuration in a documented order: explicit flag, environment variable, project config, user config, then built-in default. Use standard locations (XDG on Linux), support `--config`, validate values at startup with actionable errors, and never read or write another tool's config file. Prefer environment variables or files for secrets and support `--config -` or stdin where it avoids writing secrets to disk.

> URLs: [XDG Base Directory Specification](https://specifications.freedesktop.org/basedir-spec/latest/)

### Consistency

`cli:consistency` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Reuse one vocabulary and one behavior for common concerns across all commands. The canonical flag names and semantics live in `cli:flag-vocabulary`; never introduce a second spelling for the same concern. Keep destructive operations symmetric and predictable, accept global flags before and after subcommands, and reserve abbreviations for unambiguous prefixes. Match the platform's flag syntax conventions without inventing a private dialect.

### Feedback

`cli:feedback` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Acknowledge long operations on stderr within 100 ms and report a definite success or failure. Show progress for work over 1 s when stderr is a TTY, print a deterministic final summary, and make repeated runs idempotent. Never claim success before writes are durable and never leave a half-finished state without saying so.

### Composability

`cli:composability` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Follow the Unix philosophy: one command does one job well, reads stdin and writes stdout so it can be piped, and uses `-` for stdin where a file is expected. Support null-delimited output (`-0` or `--print0`) for filenames, avoid pagers when stdout is not a TTY, and keep machine-readable output free of locale-dependent formatting.

### Performance

`cli:performance` · scope **tech** · from *CLI Conventions*

Keep startup fast, stream results as they become available instead of buffering the whole run, and avoid network or disk work the command does not need. Bound external calls with timeouts and retries with backoff, make long operations cancelable, and never hide a slow step behind a silent pause.

## Bash

> 11 rules

### Deploy Confirmation

`bash:deploy-confirmation` · scope **tech** · from *Bash Conventions*

Every deployment script MUST print a summary of the planned actions before changing anything and ask for explicit confirmation before proceeding. The summary lists the target environment and hosts, the version/tag or commit being deployed, the services and configuration that will change, and every destructive step (migrations, deletions, restarts); it never prints secret values. Abort with a non-zero exit code unless the answer is an explicit yes. Support `-n`/`--no-interaction` to skip the prompt and proceed and `--dry-run` to print the same summary without applying it; require `--no-interaction` when stdin is not a TTY.

### Security

`bash:security` · scope **tech** · from *Bash Conventions*

Avoid using `eval`; be cautious with user-supplied input; use `readonly` for critical variables; implement proper input validation. Minimize external commands, use built-ins, check command availability, avoid bashisms if cross-shell needed, test with `shellcheck`. Include self-test mode and input validation.

### Shebang Strict

`bash:shebang-strict` · scope **tech** · from *Bash Conventions*

Always use the shebang `#!/usr/bin/env bash` for maximum portability. Enable strict error handling and safety modes at the beginning of the script: `set -euo pipefail`. Add comments explaining each option: `# -e: Exit immediately if a command exits with non-zero status`, `# -u: Treat unset variables as an error`, `# -o pipefail: Return exit status of last command in pipeline that failed`.

> Sources: Bash Conventions

### Error Handling

`bash:error-handling` · scope **tech** · from *Bash Conventions*

Define and document meaningful exit codes (0 success, 1 general, 2 misuse, 126 cannot execute, 127 not found, 128 invalid arg, 130 terminated). Consider using traps for cleanup: `trap cleanup EXIT ERR` with a cleanup function.

### Variables

`bash:variables` · scope **tech** · from *Bash Conventions*

Use `UPPERCASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES` for constants and global variables; `snake_case` for local variables; prefix internal/private variables with underscore `_internal_var`. Always quote variables to prevent word splitting and globbing. Use `readonly` for constants, `local` for function-scoped variables.

### Control Flow

`bash:control-flow` · scope **tech** · from *Bash Conventions*

Use Bash's double-bracket conditional test syntax (a pair of square brackets), prefer `==` for string comparisons, `-eq`, `-ne` etc. for integers. Use `for` loops with safe practices and quote variables in loops.

### Functions

`bash:functions` · scope **tech** · from *Bash Conventions*

Document each function with a comment block (purpose, behavior, arguments, returns, example). Keep functions small, focused, single responsibility, prefer pure functions. Use `return` for status codes (0 success, non-zero error) and command substitution `$()` for returning output.

### CLI Help

`bash:cli-help` · scope **tech** · from *Bash Conventions*

Each script should have at least `-h|--help` CLI flags and a `usage` function to document usage.

### Defaults

`bash:defaults` · scope **tech** · from *Bash Conventions*

Use parameter expansion for providing default values, e.g. `log_level="${LOG_LEVEL:-info}"` and `config_path="${1:-/default/path}"`.

### Header Comments

`bash:header-comments` · scope **tech** · from *Bash Conventions*

Include comprehensive doc header at top of each script (after shebang) with script name, creation/mod dates, detailed description, optional author and version. Write clear concise comments explaining complex logic and **why** not just **what**. Use `#` for inline comments and `# ---- ` for section comments. Use `# TODO:` for planned improvements.

### Io

`bash:io` · scope **tech** · from *Bash Conventions*

Use `echo` for standard output, `printf` for formatted output, redirect errors to `stderr` (e.g., `echo "Error: Invalid input" >&2`).

## Nodejs

> 11 rules

### Package Manager

`nodejs:package-manager` · scope **tech** · from *Node.js Conventions*

Use exactly one package manager per repository and never mix `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, and `bun` lockfiles. Declare `"packageManager": "<manager>@<version>"` in `package.json`, commit the matching lockfile, and install in CI with the frozen mode (`npm ci`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `yarn install --immutable`, or `bun install --frozen-lockfile`).

> URLs: [Node.js Packages: packageManager](https://nodejs.org/api/packages.html#packagemanager)

### Security

`nodejs:security` · scope **tech** · from *Node.js Conventions*

Treat all input as untrusted: validate at boundaries, never pass interpolated user input to `child_process.exec`, and prefer `execFile` or `spawn` with an argument array and `shell: false`. Never use `eval` or `new Function`, never bind debug inspectors to public interfaces, and run services with the least privilege and a patched dependency tree.

> URLs: [Node.js child_process](https://nodejs.org/api/child_process.html)

### Async Errors

`nodejs:async-errors` · scope **tech** · from *Node.js Conventions*

Use `async`/`await` and handle every promise: no floating promises, no async callbacks passed where a synchronous return is expected, and no `new Promise` around APIs that already return promises. Handle errors at the boundary (HTTP handler, CLI command, worker loop), attach context, set a non-zero `process.exitCode`, and use `AbortSignal.timeout()` or an explicit timeout for external calls.

> URLs: [Node.js process.exitCode](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#processexitcode)

### Environment

`nodejs:environment` · scope **tech** · from *Node.js Conventions*

Read configuration from environment variables at the process boundary, validate it once at startup, and fail fast with a message naming the missing or invalid variable. Commit `.env.example` but never `.env`; never log secrets or put server-only credentials in variables exposed to the browser.

### Lifecycle

`nodejs:lifecycle` · scope **tech** · from *Node.js Conventions*

Handle `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` by stopping new work, closing servers, database pools, queues, and streams, then letting the process exit within a bounded grace period. Do not call `process.exit()` in libraries or before flushing logs; reserve `uncaughtException` and `unhandledRejection` handlers for last-resort logging and a non-zero exit.

### Runtime

`nodejs:runtime` · scope **tech** · from *Node.js Conventions*

Target an active Node.js LTS release and pin it in `engines.node` plus `.nvmrc` or `.node-version`, and in CI (`actions/setup-node` with `node-version-file`). Use even-numbered LTS versions; do not develop against the system Node or an unmaintained EOL release, and bump the pinned version deliberately.

> URLs: [Node.js Releases](https://nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases)

### Dependencies

`nodejs:dependencies` · scope **tech** · from *Node.js Conventions*

Add dependencies deliberately and keep the tree small. Pin major versions with a committed lockfile, avoid `latest`, Git URLs, and unmaintained packages, run the package manager's audit in CI, and put shared fixes in `overrides` or `resolutions` instead of forking. Review `postinstall` scripts from untrusted packages before allowing them.

### Modules

`nodejs:modules` · scope **tech** · from *Node.js Conventions*

Use ES modules for new code: set `"type": "module"`, use `import`/`export`, and import Node built-ins with the `node:` prefix (`node:fs/promises`, `node:path`). Do not mix `require` and `import` in the same module tree; if CommonJS interoperability is required, isolate it behind one adapter and configure `exports` explicitly.

> URLs: [Node.js ES Modules](https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html)

### Manifest

`nodejs:manifest` · scope **tech** · from *Node.js Conventions*

Keep `package.json` small and explicit: `name`, `version`, `private` for applications, `engines`, `packageManager`, and scripts for `dev`, `build`, `test`, `lint`, and `typecheck`. Put runtime libraries in `dependencies` and build/test tooling in `devDependencies`; expose behavior through scripts instead of requiring globally installed tools.

> URLs: [package.json](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/configuring-npm/package-json)

### Testing

`nodejs:testing` · scope **tech** · from *Node.js Conventions*

Test behavior through the project's standard runner (`node:test` or the configured Vitest/Jest setup) and keep tests deterministic: no real network, no shared global state, and temporary directories for filesystem work. Cover error paths, timeouts, and cancellation as well as the happy path, and run the suite in CI with the pinned Node version.

> URLs: [Node.js test runner](https://nodejs.org/api/test.html)

### Logging

`nodejs:logging` · scope **tech** · from *Node.js Conventions*

Use a structured logger (for example `pino`) instead of `console.log` in application code; write diagnostics to stderr and keep machine output on stdout. Log at boundaries with stable fields (request id, job id, duration) and redact secrets, tokens, and personal data. Never log whole request bodies, and never make a stack trace the only error signal.

## Rust

> 11 rules

### Unsafe Policy

`rust:unsafe-policy` · scope **tech** · from *Rust Conventions*

`unsafe` is forbidden by default; add `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` to new crates. When unavoidable, isolate it behind the smallest safe abstraction, justify every block with a `// SAFETY:` comment stating the invariant, and cover it with tests and `miri` where practical. Never use `unsafe` to silence the borrow checker.

### Error Handling

`rust:error-handling` · scope **tech** · from *Rust Conventions*

Return `Result<T, E>`; never `panic!`, `unwrap()`, or `expect()` on recoverable paths. Libraries define typed errors with `thiserror`; binaries may use `anyhow` at the boundary. Add context with `map_err` or `anyhow::Context` and propagate with `?`. Mark public error enums `#[non_exhaustive]` and implement `std::error::Error`.

### Concurrency Async

`rust:concurrency-async` · scope **tech** · from *Rust Conventions*

Prefer message passing and scoped tasks over shared mutable state; use `Mutex` or `RwLock` only for short critical sections and never hold a lock across `.await`. In async code never block the executor with `std::thread::sleep` or blocking I/O; use `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`. Bound channels and task counts, and propagate cancellation.

### Toolchain

`rust:toolchain` · scope **tech** · from *Rust Conventions*

Target the latest stable Rust and pin it in `rust-toolchain.toml`. Set `edition` (2024 for new crates) and `rust-version` (MSRV) in `Cargo.toml`. CI must run `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`; do not merge warnings.

### API Design

`rust:api-design` · scope **tech** · from *Rust Conventions*

Accept borrowed inputs (`&str`, `&[T]`, `impl AsRef<Path>`) and return owned values. Prefer iterators and `impl Trait` over intermediate collections, and avoid needless `clone()`, `Rc<RefCell<_>>`, and premature lifetime annotations. Use newtypes for domain ids and units; derive `Debug`, `Clone`, `PartialEq`, and `Eq` where meaningful.

### Testing

`rust:testing` · scope **tech** · from *Rust Conventions*

Unit tests live in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` next to the code; integration tests in `tests/` exercise only the public API. Use `#[test]` or `#[tokio::test]` and `assert_eq!` with descriptive messages. Cover error paths and edge cases, not only the happy path. Doctests on public items must compile. Run `cargo test --all-features` (or `cargo nextest run`) in CI.

### Dependencies

`rust:dependencies` · scope **tech** · from *Rust Conventions*

Keep dependencies minimal and feature-gated (`default-features = false` where possible); justify every new crate. Commit `Cargo.lock` for binaries but not for libraries. Run `cargo audit` or `cargo deny check` in CI and avoid duplicate major versions in the dependency tree where practical.

### Documentation

`rust:documentation` · scope **tech** · from *Rust Conventions*

Document every public item with `///` and modules with `//!`, including panics, errors, and safety invariants; enable `#![warn(missing_docs)]` for libraries. Provide a crate-level example that compiles as a doctest and keep `README.md` and `cargo doc` output current.

### Observability

`rust:observability` · scope **tech** · from *Rust Conventions*

Use `tracing` with `tracing-subscriber` instead of `println!` or `eprintln!` for diagnostics; emit structured fields rather than interpolated strings. Log at boundaries (commands, handlers, I/O) and never log secrets or full user payloads.

### Project Structure

`rust:project-structure` · scope **tech** · from *Rust Conventions*

Split multi-crate workspaces into `crates/<name>/` with a thin `src/main.rs` that parses arguments and delegates to `lib.rs`. Organize modules by domain, not by type, and prefer `foo.rs` plus `foo/` over `mod.rs` in new code. Put shared metadata and lints in the workspace `Cargo.toml`.

### Style Naming

`rust:style-naming` · scope **tech** · from *Rust Conventions*

Follow RFC 430 and the Rust API Guidelines: `snake_case` for functions, variables, modules, and files; `PascalCase` for types, traits, and enum variants; `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants and statics. Treat acronyms as words (`HttpClient`, not `HTTPClient`). Use `cargo fmt` as the only formatter and never hand-format code.

> URLs: [Rust API Guidelines](https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/)

## Tauri

> 12 rules

### Security Boundary

`tauri:security-boundary` · scope **tech** · from *Tauri Conventions*

Treat the webview as untrusted: re-validate every argument in Rust (paths, ids, sizes, URLs), never expose raw filesystem, shell, or database access, and never ship secrets, tokens, or private keys in frontend code or `VITE_*` variables. Deny by default and prefer official `tauri-plugin-*` crates over custom bridges.

> URLs: [Tauri Security](https://v2.tauri.app/security/)

### Updater Signing

`tauri:updater-signing` · scope **tech** · from *Tauri Conventions*

Ship updates only through the signed updater: generate a key pair, keep the private key and password in CI secrets (never in the repository), put only the public key in `tauri.conf.json`, and publish signed artifacts with a `latest.json` manifest over HTTPS.

> URLs: [Tauri Updater Plugin](https://v2.tauri.app/plugin/updater/)

### Csp

`tauri:csp` · scope **tech** · from *Tauri Conventions*

Keep a strict Content Security Policy in `app.security.csp`; never disable it or set `dangerousDisableAssetCspModification`. Avoid `unsafe-inline` and `unsafe-eval`, load remote content only from allow-listed origins, and prefer bundled assets. Set `freezePrototype` where the platform supports it.

> URLs: [Tauri Content Security Policy](https://v2.tauri.app/security/csp/)

### Capabilities

`tauri:capabilities` · scope **tech** · from *Tauri Conventions*

Use Tauri 2 capabilities (`src-tauri/capabilities/*.json`) with least privilege: one capability per window or feature, explicit permission lists, and no blanket `core:default` where a narrower set works. Keep `withGlobalTauri` disabled and review every added permission as a security change.

> URLs: [Tauri Capabilities](https://v2.tauri.app/security/capabilities/)

### Ipc Contract

`tauri:ipc-contract` · scope **tech** · from *Tauri Conventions*

Every command takes and returns explicit `serde`-serializable DTOs (`CreateProjectRequest`, `ProjectDto`), never tuples or `serde_json::Value`. Return `Result<T, CommandError>` where `CommandError: Serialize` is a tagged enum with stable `code` and `message` fields; the frontend maps `code` to localized copy. Keep commands async and do not hold locks across `.await`.

### Architecture

`tauri:architecture` · scope **tech** · from *Tauri Conventions*

Keep the Rust side a service layer: `src-tauri/src/commands/` holds thin `#[tauri::command]` handlers that validate input and delegate to plain Rust modules (`services/`, `domain/`); no window or UI logic in services. The frontend calls commands only through one typed wrapper module, never `invoke()` scattered across components.

> URLs: [Tauri: Calling Rust from the Frontend](https://v2.tauri.app/develop/calling-rust/)

### State

`tauri:state` · scope **tech** · from *Tauri Conventions*

Manage shared state through `tauri::State` with a single owner (`AppState`); use `Mutex`, `RwLock`, or an actor/channel for mutation and keep lock scopes short. Initialize state in `setup`, fail fast on database or migration errors, and persist user settings with `tauri-plugin-store` rather than ad-hoc JSON files.

### Cross Platform

`tauri:cross-platform` · scope **tech** · from *Tauri Conventions*

Build and smoke-test on every supported OS in CI (Windows WebView2, macOS WKWebView, Linux WebKitGTK), and document Linux system dependencies. Isolate platform differences (paths, menus, shortcuts, decorations) behind `#[cfg(target_os)]`, and verify high-DPI scaling and window resizing.

### Events

`tauri:events` · scope **tech** · from *Tauri Conventions*

Use events for backend-to-frontend notifications and channels for high-volume streams; define event names and payload types in one shared module on each side. Do not poll the backend when an event is available, and unsubscribe listeners when components unmount.

### Testing

`tauri:testing` · scope **tech** · from *Tauri Conventions*

Test command handlers and services as plain Rust functions with `#[test]` or `#[tokio::test]`; use `tauri::test::mock_builder` with `MockRuntime` for IPC integration tests. Frontend tests mock the typed command wrapper, not `invoke` directly. Add an end-to-end smoke test per release on each supported OS.

### Config

`tauri:config` · scope **tech** · from *Tauri Conventions*

Commit `src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` with a stable reverse-DNS `identifier`, `productName`, semantic `version`, and explicit `bundle.targets`. Wire `build.beforeDevCommand`, `beforeBuildCommand`, `devUrl`, and `frontendDist` to the frontend toolchain; keep machine-specific paths and secrets out of the file.

> URLs: [Tauri Configuration Reference](https://v2.tauri.app/reference/config/)

### Logging

`tauri:logging` · scope **tech** · from *Tauri Conventions*

Log command entry, exit, and failures with `tracing`; never log payloads containing secrets or personal data. Return user-safe messages to the frontend while keeping technical detail in logs, and report panics through `tauri-plugin-log` or an error-tracking service.

## UI

> 15 rules

### Accessibility

`ui:accessibility` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Meet WCAG 2.2 AA: semantic elements and roles, accessible names for every control, visible focus, full keyboard operability, logical focus order, and 4.5:1 text contrast. Never remove focus outlines; respect `prefers-reduced-motion`; verify with keyboard-only use and a screen reader.

> URLs: [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/), [ARIA Authoring Practices Guide](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/)

### Component Package

`ui:component-package` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Every UI surface uses exactly one approved kit from `packages/ui-component-registry.yaml` for its medium and stack. A kit is a UI implementation (webview, CLI, TUI), not an app-wide choice: an app may use different kits on different surfaces (for example TradeGuard uses Vuetify + `Tdx*` for its web UI, CliStyle for console commands, and PhpTui for dashboards). New web/Tauri surfaces use `@topdata-software-gmbh/ui`; new Go TUI and Symfony console surfaces use their registered kits (`topdata-tui-go`, `topdata-console-php`). If the registered kit is still `planned`, coordinate with its owner and register the surface instead of creating an unregistered local kit. Never mix kits on one surface. Do not copy, fork, wrap-and-restyle, or override a primitive's internals; extend the chosen kit through documented props, slots, or helpers and shared design tokens. If a primitive is missing or insufficient, add it to that kit with tests, docs, and a playground entry rather than creating a local variant. Pin a released version and commit the lockfile.

> Sources: TopData UI kit registry

### Errors

`ui:errors` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Error copy states what happened, why, and what to do next, in plain language; never expose stack traces, unexplained codes, or blame the user. Log technical detail, show a support reference id, and preserve the user's context (no data loss, no dead ends).

### States

`ui:states` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Every view handles five states explicitly: loading, empty, error, partial or offline, and success. Prefer skeletons over spinners for content, disable submit controls while a request is in flight, and always offer a recovery action (retry, back, edit).

### Feedback

`ui:feedback` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Acknowledge every user action within 100 ms (pressed, disabled, or optimistic state) and report outcomes within 1 s. Use inline messages for field- and context-level problems, toasts for transient confirmations, and reserve modals for blocking decisions. Confirm destructive actions and make them undoable where possible.

### Forms

`ui:forms` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Label every field visibly (never use a placeholder as the label), mark required fields, validate on blur and submit with inline messages next to the field, preserve entered values on error, and set correct `type`, `inputmode`, and `autocomplete` attributes. Focus the first invalid field and let Enter submit single-line forms.

### Package Governance

`ui:package-governance` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Approved UI kits are registered in `packages/ui-component-registry.yaml` with kit id, medium, stack, owner, package or in-repo source, version, status, and consuming surfaces. Adding a kit, moving a surface to another kit, or changing ownership requires an ADR and a registry entry. An app's project ruleset must name the kit for each surface. Do not create a second kit for an existing surface, and do not migrate a legacy surface as part of unrelated work.

> Sources: TopData UI kit registry

### Consistency

`ui:consistency` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Reuse existing components and patterns before creating new ones, and keep interaction, terminology, and placement consistent across screens. New components belong in the shared design system with default, hover, focus, active, disabled, and loading states plus a documented API.

### Layout

`ui:layout` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Design mobile-first with a consistent 4 or 8 px spacing scale, a constrained readable line length (45-75 characters), and layouts that reflow without horizontal scrolling. Touch targets are at least 44x44 px; content respects safe areas, 200% zoom, and long or localized strings.

### Navigation

`ui:navigation` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Keep navigation predictable: persistent primary navigation, visible current location, breadcrumbs for deep hierarchies, and a working back path. Guard unsaved changes before leaving, preserve scroll and filter state on return, and make deep links shareable for web views.

### Design Tokens

`ui:design-tokens` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Centralize color, spacing, typography, radius, shadow, and motion values as design tokens (CSS custom properties or a theme object); components consume tokens and never hard-code hex or pixel values. Support light and dark themes through tokens and keep iconography from one consistent set.

### Desktop

`ui:desktop` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Desktop windows must be resizable with a sensible minimum size, remember window size and position, and expose standard keyboard shortcuts and a native menu where appropriate. Never rely on hover-only affordances; support keyboard, trackpad, and high-DPI displays.

### I18n

`ui:i18n` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Never hard-code user-facing strings; externalize them with interpolation and pluralization support, and use locale-aware date, time, number, and currency formatting. Design for text expansion (up to about 35%) and RTL mirroring; keep icons and layout direction-aware.

### Performance Perception

`ui:performance-perception` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Render above-the-fold content first, reserve space to avoid layout shift, virtualize long lists, debounce expensive input, and lazy-load non-critical assets. Show progress for operations over 1 s and never block the whole interface for a background task.

### Typography

`ui:typography` · scope **tech** · from *UI/UX Conventions*

Use a small, fixed type scale (for example 12/14/16/20/24/32) with a system font stack, line-height 1.4-1.6 for body text, and no more than two font families. Never convey information by color, size, or position alone; pair it with text, an icon, or a shape.

## Vite

> 10 rules

### Environment

`vite:environment` · scope **tech** · from *Vite Conventions*

Expose only `VITE_`-prefixed variables to client code via `import.meta.env`; never put secrets, API tokens, or server credentials there because they are embedded in the bundle. Keep `.env`, `.env.local`, and mode-specific files out of git, commit `.env.example`, and validate required variables at startup or build time.

> URLs: [Vite: Env Variables and Modes](https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode)

### Dev Server

`vite:dev-server` · scope **tech** · from *Vite Conventions*

Never run Vite on the default port `5173` (reserved as a trap default); claim a reserved frontend port from `~/devel/port-map/ports-private.yaml` (`518x`) or `ports-topdata.yaml` and set it in `server.port` with `strictPort: true`. Bind `server.host` explicitly and do not expose the dev server on a public interface.

> URLs: [Vite Server Options](https://vite.dev/config/server-options)

### Typescript

`vite:typescript` · scope **tech** · from *Vite Conventions*

Use `vite.config.ts` with TypeScript and commit `src/vite-env.d.ts` containing `/// <reference types="vite/client" />`; extend `ImportMetaEnv` for every custom `VITE_` variable. Run `tsc --noEmit` (or the project's typecheck script) in CI because Vite transpiles without type checking.

> URLs: [Vite: TypeScript](https://vite.dev/guide/features#typescript)

### Build

`vite:build` · scope **tech** · from *Vite Conventions*

Set `build.outDir` outside source directories (for example `dist/`) and keep it gitignored; use `emptyOutDir` only for directories Vite owns. Set `base` to the real deployment path, enable source maps only when the deployment protects them, and rely on Vite's hashed filenames instead of manual cache-busting.

> URLs: [Vite Build Options](https://vite.dev/config/build-options)

### Proxy

`vite:proxy` · scope **tech** · from *Vite Conventions*

Proxy backend APIs through `server.proxy` during development instead of disabling browser security or adding CORS bypasses to the backend. Read the target from the environment, set `changeOrigin` deliberately, rewrite only the path prefix, and keep the same public path in production so client code does not branch on environment.

> URLs: [Vite: server.proxy](https://vite.dev/config/server-options#server-proxy)

### Config

`vite:config` · scope **tech** · from *Vite Conventions*

Keep one `vite.config.ts` at the project root and export it with `defineConfig` (or `defineConfig(({ mode }) => ...)` only when behavior truly depends on mode). Keep aliases, plugins, and build settings in that file; do not scatter Vite configuration across scripts or duplicate it in framework configs.

> URLs: [Vite Config Reference](https://vite.dev/config/)

### Plugins

`vite:plugins` · scope **tech** · from *Vite Conventions*

Prefer official or actively maintained Vite plugins and configure each one once; do not add two plugins that compile the same language or duplicate an existing framework integration. Keep plugin order explicit, pass only the options the project needs, and avoid Node-only plugins or polyfills in code that runs in the browser.

> URLs: [Vite Plugins](https://vite.dev/plugins/)

### Testing

`vite:testing` · scope **tech** · from *Vite Conventions*

Use Vitest with the same Vite config (`defineConfig` from `vitest/config`) so aliases, environment variables, and plugins match the app. Prefer `environment: 'node'` for pure logic and add jsdom or happy-dom only for DOM tests; reset mocks between tests and run the suite in CI.

> URLs: [Vitest Configuration](https://vitest.dev/config/)

### Assets

`vite:assets` · scope **tech** · from *Vite Conventions*

Import assets from JavaScript or CSS so Vite fingerprints and rewrites them; reserve `public/` for files that must keep a stable URL (favicons, `robots.txt`, externally referenced downloads). Use `?url` or `?raw` for explicit handling, avoid hard-coded `/src/...` paths, and reference public assets from the configured `base` rather than the filesystem root.

> URLs: [Vite: Static Asset Handling](https://vite.dev/guide/assets)

### Performance

`vite:performance` · scope **tech** · from *Vite Conventions*

Keep the initial bundle small: lazy-load routes and heavy features with dynamic `import()`, import only the modules you use instead of barrel files, and add large CommonJS dependencies to `optimizeDeps.include` only when pre-bundling is actually needed. Measure with `vite build --debug` or a bundle analyzer before adding manual chunk rules.

> URLs: [Vite: Building for Production](https://vite.dev/guide/build)

## Docs

> 15 rules

### Environment Variables

`docs:environment-variables` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

Any project that reads environment variables MUST maintain `/docs/environment-variables.md`. Document every variable in one table with: name, purpose, type and default, required or optional, whether it is secret, a safe example value, and where it is read or which component uses it. Keep the file in sync with the code in the same change, make `.env.example` match it, and describe startup validation and failure behavior. Never write real secrets into the file.

### Code Docstrings

`docs:code-docstrings` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

Every public or exported module, class, function, method, and type has a docstring in the language's convention (PEP 257, TSDoc/JSDoc, Go doc comments, rustdoc `///`, PHPDoc). Document the contract, not the implementation: purpose, parameters and their units or ranges, return value, raised errors, side effects, and thread-safety. Do not repeat information already carried by the type signature. Add a docstring to private code when its contract or algorithm is not obvious from the name and signature.

### Maintenance

`docs:maintenance` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

Treat documentation as part of the change: update affected docs in the same commit or pull request, delete stale content instead of leaving it, and verify links and commands in CI (link checker, docs build, quick-start smoke test). Assign an owner or reviewer for docs and review them at release time.

### Minimum Set

`docs:minimum-set` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

Every project maintains a small documentation set rooted at `README.md` and `/docs/`: `README.md` (entry point), `/docs/architecture.md`, `/docs/development.md`, and `CHANGELOG.md`. Add `/docs/environment-variables.md` when the project reads environment variables, `/docs/operations.md` when it is deployed or operated as a service, `/docs/api.md` (or a generated spec) when it exposes an API, and ADRs under `_ai/technical_decisions/` for significant decisions. Link every document from the README and never create empty placeholder files.

### Changelog

`docs:changelog` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

Keep `CHANGELOG.md` in Keep a Changelog format with an `Unreleased` section and SemVer versions. Group entries under Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, and Security; write them for users, link issues or pull requests, and never rewrite released entries. Update the changelog in the same pull request as the change.

> URLs: [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/)

### Code Comments

`docs:code-comments` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

Comments explain intent, constraints, trade-offs, and why the code is written this way — never restate what the code already says. Keep a comment next to the code it describes and update or delete it in the same change. Never leave commented-out code; delete it and rely on version control. Mark known debt with `TODO` or `FIXME` plus an owner or issue reference. Use the language's comment syntax and the project's existing section markers consistently.

### Development

`docs:development` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

`/docs/development.md` (or `CONTRIBUTING.md`) gives exact, tested commands for prerequisites, first-time setup, running locally, tests, lint, typecheck, build, and release. State required tool versions and how to seed or reset local data. Keep commands copy-pasteable and update them in the same change that alters the workflow.

### Readme

`docs:readme` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

The README is the entry point and must cover, in order: what the project does and who it is for, prerequisites, installation, a copy-pasteable quick start, configuration (link to `/docs/environment-variables.md`), development and test commands (link to `/docs/development.md`), and the license. Keep it short and move detail into `/docs/` with links.

### Adr

`docs:adr` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

Record significant, hard-to-reverse decisions as ADRs in the project's ADR directory (`_ai/technical_decisions/` in these repositories) with status, context, decision, consequences, and alternatives considered. Follow the repository's existing filename and numbering pattern, never delete or rewrite accepted ADRs, and supersede one with a new ADR that cross-links both.

### API

`docs:api` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

Any project that exposes an API (HTTP, IPC, CLI, or library) must document its contract in `/docs/api.md` or a generated spec (OpenAPI, JSON Schema, or rustdoc). Cover authentication, request and response examples, error codes and their meaning, pagination and limits, versioning, and the deprecation policy.

### Architecture

`docs:architecture` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

`/docs/architecture.md` explains the system at a glance: context and goals, major components and their responsibilities, boundaries and data flow, key runtime dependencies, and important trade-offs. Include a text-based diagram (Mermaid preferred) that is versioned with the code, and link ADRs for decisions instead of duplicating their rationale.

### Code Examples

`docs:code-examples` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

Every non-obvious public API has a short, runnable example with realistic identifiers and values and its expected output. Run examples in CI (doctest, an `examples/` directory, or a snippet test) so they cannot rot. Mark examples that cannot run as illustrative and keep them out of the test harness.

### Code Reference

`docs:code-reference` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

Generate the API reference from source annotations and docstrings with the language's standard tool (Sphinx/autodoc, TypeDoc, rustdoc, godoc, phpDocumentor); never maintain a parallel hand-written reference. Version the generator configuration with the code, fail CI when the documentation build breaks, and link the generated reference from `README.md` and `/docs/`. Hand-written guides may explain the reference but must not duplicate signatures.

### Operations

`docs:operations` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

Deployable services maintain `/docs/operations.md`: environments and topology, deploy and rollback procedure, configuration and secret injection, database migrations, backup and restore, health checks, monitoring and alerting, and a troubleshooting table of symptom to cause to action. Include the exact commands and expected output for each runbook step.

### Style

`docs:style` · scope **global** · from *Documentation Conventions*

Write documentation in plain language, present tense, active voice, and second person. Use descriptive headings, short paragraphs, fenced code blocks with a language tag, and relative links that work in the repository. Prefer text over screenshots for commands and configuration; date version-specific statements and state prerequisites before steps.

## Release

> 2 rules

### Git Tags

`release:git-tags` · scope **global** · from *Release & Versioning Conventions*

Publish releases as annotated Git tags named `v<MAJOR>.<MINOR>.<PATCH>` (for example `v1.4.0`), with `-alpha.N`, `-beta.N`, or `-rc.N` for pre-releases. Tag the exact commit that produced the published artifact, sign tags where possible (`git tag -s`), and push them explicitly with `git push origin <tag>`. Never move, force-update, or delete a published tag; publish a new version instead. The tag name must match the version in the package manifest and changelog.

> URLs: [git-tag documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-tag)

### Semver

`release:semver` · scope **global** · from *Release & Versioning Conventions*

Version numbers follow Semantic Versioning 2.0.0: `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. Bump MAJOR for incompatible changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, and PATCH for backward-compatible fixes. Pre-releases use `-alpha.N`, `-beta.N`, or `-rc.N`; build metadata uses `+...` and never affects precedence. Keep one source of truth for the version and make package manifests, app metadata, changelog entries, and release artifacts agree.

> URLs: [Semantic Versioning 2.0.0](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html)
